result.prose:
# 100 Hz Bone-Conducted Tone Reduces Motion Sickness via Otolith Stimulation; VR Relevance Is Inferred from a Driving-Simulator Proxy

**Answer.** A 2025 Nagoya University study (82 participants) demonstrated that a 1-minute, 100 Hz pure tone delivered binaurally at 80–85 dBZ reduces motion-sickness symptoms by physically vibrating the otoconia in the inner ear, with improved posturography and reduced sympathetic activation across three motion scenarios—including a driving simulator explicitly described as modeling the VR cybersickness mechanism [Source 5, 6, 7, 10]. The evidence establishes the mechanism and general anti-vestibular-conflict efficacy, but the retrieved sources do not include a controlled trial applying the tone inside an actual VR headset, so quantitative effectiveness for VR-specific cybersickness remains an inference rather than a measured outcome.

## What the evidence supports

- **Mechanism.** 100 Hz is the resonant frequency of otoconia (calcium-carbonate crystals) in the utricle and saccule; bone-conducted sound at this frequency vibrates the crystals and provides supplementary vestibular input to the brain [Source 5, 6, 7].
- **Human efficacy.** In 82 participants across a mechanical swing, a 360° driving simulator, and a real vehicle, 1-minute pre-exposure to the 100 Hz tone improved posturography envelope areas (reduced sway) in all three scenarios and reduced driving-simulator sympathetic activation (HRV) and vehicle MSAQ scores [Source 5, 6, 7, 10].
- **VR proxy.** The driving-simulator condition (visual road motion + stationary body) was described as "the same mechanism that causes cybersickness in VR," making it the closest tested analogue to a headset experience [Source 5].
- **Frequency and intensity specificity (mouse).** In ex vivo murine utricle explants, only 100 Hz at 75–85 dBZ for 5 min produced a vestibular response; 90, 250, 500, and 1000 Hz, and levels below 75 dBZ, did not. Surgically removing the otoliths eliminated the 100 Hz response, confirming the otoliths—not the cochlea—as the target [Source 7].
- **Binaural delivery is required.** Exposure to only one ear produced no effect; a verified design used two speakers 10 cm left and right of a headrest [Source 7].
- **Greater benefit for susceptible users.** The effect was stronger in participants originally prone to motion sickness; no significant difference appeared in less-prone participants [Source 7].
- **Causal role of vestibular conflict confirmed independently.** A GVS study (10 participants) showed "beneficial" GVS reduced motion sickness by 26% and "detrimental" GVS increased it by 56% (p = 0.0055), supporting the sensory-conflict model that the 100 Hz tone targets [Source 2].
- **VR cybersickness mechanism.** Cybersickness arises from a visual–vestibular–proprioceptive mismatch integrated in the brainstem and cerebellum; an EEG study (14 subjects) showed increased slow-wave (1–10 Hz) activity in temporo-occipital regions as mismatch and VIMS severity grew [Source 1, 11, 12, 15].
- **Practical parameters.** 100 Hz pure tone, 80–85 dBZ (≈61–66 dBA, roughly conversational volume), binaural, 1 minute before the motion stimulus, in a quiet environment [Source 3, 4, 7, 10].
- **No hearing damage detected.** Distortion-product otoacoustic emissions showed no effect; the exposure level is well below WHO occupational noise limits [Source 6, 7].
- **Commercial and developer uptake.** Samsung reportedly integrated the findings into its Galaxy Health "Hearapy" feature, and independent developers (e.g., RideCalm) built dedicated 100 Hz tone apps [Source 5].
- **Inferred VR use-case.** Theoretically, a 1-minute binaural 100 Hz tone could be embedded as a pre-session "calibration" step in a VR application, delivered via headset speakers or external headphones, to prime the vestibular system before the user enters the virtual environment [Source 3, 4, 5, 7, 10].

## What was not found

- Was the 100 Hz tone ever applied inside an actual VR headset (e.g., Quest, Vive) with cybersickness outcomes measured in a controlled trial?
- What VR-specific developer guidance exists—integration APIs, timing relative to scene transitions, interaction with frame-rate or refresh-rate settings, continuous versus pulsed delivery during the session?
- What is the precise neurophysiological pathway by which supplementary otolith vibration attenuates the visual-vestibular prediction error in the brainstem/cerebellum during VR, beyond the general statement that it "broadly activates the vestibular system"?
- Has any source compared 100 Hz sound stimulation head-to-head against pharmacological antiemetics or other non-pharmacological countermeasures (GVS, fluid-filled glasses) within the same VR context?

result.synthesis:
[UNCERTAIN] A 2025 study by Nagoya University (Gu, Kagawa, Kato, et al.), published in *Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine* (Vol. 30, Article 22, DOI: 10.1265/ehpm.24-00247), demonstrated that a 1-minute exposure to a pure 100 Hz tone at 80–85 dBZ (≈60.9–65.9 dBA) before motion exposure reduced motion sickness symptoms in humans. (unverified figure: 24, 65.9) [Source 3, 10]
[SOURCED] The mechanism is that 100 Hz is the resonant frequency of the otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) in the otolith organs (utricle and saccule) of the inner ear; sound at this frequency, delivered via bone conduction through headphones, physically vibrates the otoconia and provides supplementary vestibular input to the brain. [Source 5, 6, 7]
[UNCERTAIN] In ex vivo murine utricle explant experiments, only 100 Hz at 75–85 dBZ for 5 minutes produced a vestibular response; no reaction was observed at 90 Hz, 250 Hz, 500 Hz, or 1000 Hz, and no reaction occurred below 75 dBZ. (unverified figure: 5) [Source 7]
[SOURCED] When the otoliths were surgically removed from the mouse tissue, the 100 Hz–induced activation disappeared, confirming that the otoliths (not the cochlea) were the target of the sound stimulation. [Source 7]
[SOURCED] The 100 Hz stimulation broadly activates the vestibular system, which is responsible for maintaining balance and spatial orientation, and reduces the autonomic dysregulation (excessive sympathetic activation) associated with motion sickness. [Source 6, 7]
[SOURCED] The human study used 82 participants across three motion scenarios: a mechanical swing (pendulum motion), a 360-degree driving simulator, and a real vehicle driven on a course with curves. [Source 5, 6, 7, 10]
[SOURCED] The driving simulator scenario specifically created a visual-vestibular conflict (participants saw a moving road while their bodies remained stationary), described as "the same mechanism that causes cybersickness in VR." [Source 5]
[SOURCED] Outcomes were measured objectively via posturography (center-of-gravity sway / envelope areas) and electrocardiography (heart rate variability, LF/HF ratio), and subjectively via the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire (MSAQ). [Source 6, 7, 10]
[UNCERTAIN] In the mouse model, a 5-minute exposure to 85 dBZ at 100 Hz before shaking produced a long-lasting (≥120 min) alleviative effect on beam-balance test scores. (unverified figure: 85, 120) [Source 10]
[SOURCED] In humans, 1-minute pre-exposure to the 100 Hz tone improved posturography envelope areas (reduced sway) across all three motion scenarios (swing, driving simulator, vehicle). [Source 10]
[SOURCED] Driving-simulator-mediated sympathetic nerve activation (assessed by HRV) and vehicle-mediated MSAQ scores were both improved by the pure-tone exposure. [Source 10]
[SOURCED] The beneficial effect was stronger in participants who were originally prone to motion sickness; no significant difference was observed in participants less prone to sickness. [Source 7]
[SOURCED] The sound must be delivered equally to both ears; exposure to only one ear did not produce an effect. A design with two speakers placed 10 cm to the left and right of a car headrest was verified in the study. [Source 7]
[UNCERTAIN] No effect on hearing was detected via distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAE), and the 1-minute exposure at 80–85 dBZ is well below WHO occupational noise safety limits (100 Hz at 85 dB(A) is acceptable for up to 480 minutes). (unverified figure: 480) [Source 6, 7]
[SOURCED] The study was registered under UMIN000022413 (2016/05/23–2023/04/19) and UMIN000053735 (2024/02/29–present). [Source 10]
[SOURCED] One of the sub-experiments in the study had a sample size of only 10 participants, which was noted as a limitation by community reviewers. [Source 9]
[SOURCED] VR motion sickness (cybersickness / VIMS) is attributed to a sensory conflict or mismatch between visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive signals integrated in the brainstem and cerebellum; in VR, the eyes perceive self-motion while the vestibular system detects stillness. [Source 1, 11, 12, 15]
[SOURCED] An EEG study of 14 healthy subjects in a VR environment found that with increasing visual-vestibular mismatch and subjective VIMS, the proportion of slow EEG waves (especially 1–10 Hz) increases, particularly in temporo-occipital regions, and information flow decreases in brain areas involved in vestibular signal processing. [Source 1]
[SOURCED] A GVS (galvanic vestibular stimulation) study in 10 participants showed that "Beneficial" GVS produced a 26% motion sickness reduction and "Detrimental" GVS produced a 56% increase (p = 0.0055), confirming the causal role of vestibular sensory conflict, and the authors stated the findings "facilitate new methods and countermeasures for mitigating motion sickness during transportation and in virtual environments." [Source 2]
[SOURCED] Samsung reportedly incorporated the Nagoya University findings into its Galaxy Health ecosystem under a feature called "Hearapy," and independent developers (including RideCalm) built dedicated apps to deliver the 100 Hz tone. [Source 5]
[SOURCED] The researchers plan to further develop the technology for practical application in a variety of travel situations including air and sea travel, and the sound could be incorporated into existing devices such as hearing aids and other audio devices. [Source 6, 8]
[UNCERTAIN] Recommended practical parameters from the study: 100 Hz pure tone, 80–85 dBZ (≈60.9–65.9 dBA, roughly conversational volume), delivered binaurally (both ears) for 1 minute before the motion stimulus, in a quiet environment. (unverified figure: 1) [Source 3, 4, 7, 10]
[SOURCED] Slow, intermittent exposure to motion and reducing physical, mental, or emotional discomfort are recommended general preventive strategies for motion sickness. [Source 13]
[SOURCED] A clinical study of 30 motion-sickness-susceptible participants evaluated fluid-filled glasses (creating an artificial moving horizon) against a placebo group in a CAREN (computer-assisted rehabilitation) environment, measuring symptoms with the MSAQ before, after, and at 60-second intervals. [Source 14, 16]
[INFERRED] Because the 100 Hz mechanism targets the vestibular (otolith) component of the sensory conflict, and VR cybersickness is driven by a visual-vestibular mismatch, the 100 Hz pre-exposure could theoretically reduce the vestibular "error signal" that contributes to VR-induced motion sickness, even though the visual stimulus in VR is the primary driver of the conflict. [Source 1, 5, 6, 11, 12]
[INFERRED] The driving-simulator scenario in the Nagoya study (visual motion + stationary body) is the closest proxy to VR cybersickness among the three tested conditions, but it is not identical to a full VR headset experience (which adds stereoscopic depth, head-tracked rendering, and vergence-accommodation conflict). [Source 5, 11, 12]
[UNCERTAIN] For VR developers, the practical implication is that a 1-minute binaural 100 Hz tone at ~61–66 dBA could be embedded as a pre-session "calibration" step in a VR application, delivered through the headset's built-in speakers or external headphones, to prime the vestibular system before the user enters the virtual environment. (unverified figure: 61, 66) [Source 3, 4, 5, 7, 10]
[UNCERTAIN] The long-term (beyond 120 minutes) efficacy in humans is not established; the ≥120 min duration was demonstrated only in the mouse beam-balance model, and the human studies measured symptoms during a single motion exposure session. (unverified figure: 120) [Source 10]
[UNCERTAIN] Whether the 100 Hz effect is additive with other VR-specific countermeasures (e.g., high frame rates, reduced artificial locomotion, vignetting) is not addressed in any provided source. (unverified figure: 100) [Source 11, 12]
[GAP] No source in the provided set reports a controlled experiment that directly applied the 100 Hz tone inside a VR headset environment (e.g., Oculus Quest, HTC Vive) and measured cybersickness outcomes, so the specific quantitative effectiveness of 100 Hz sound for VR-induced motion sickness remains unverified.
[GAP] No source provides VR-specific developer guidance such as recommended integration APIs, timing relative to scene transitions, interaction with frame-rate or refresh-rate settings, or whether the tone should be continuous or pulsed during the VR session.
[GAP] The precise neurophysiological pathway by which supplementary otolith vibration resolves (or attenuates) the visual-vestibular prediction error in the brainstem/cerebellum during VR is not detailed in any provided source beyond the general statement that it "broadly activates the vestibular system."
[GAP] No source reports a head-to-head comparison of 100 Hz sound stimulation versus pharmacological antiemetics (e.g., scopolamine, dimenhydrinate) or versus other non-pharmacological VR countermeasures (e.g., GVS, fluid-filled glasses) in the same VR context.

reuse_claims.text: Human studies have found that low-frequency oscillations of 0.2 Hz with large amplitudes are most likely to cause motion sickness, while at frequencies of 2 Hz or above, motion sickness ceases completely.
The GVS study explicitly states its findings "facilitate new methods and countermeasures for mitigating motion sickness during transportation and in virtual environments."
An EEG study of 14 healthy subjects in a VR environment found that with increasing visual-vestibular mismatch and subjective VIMS, the proportion of slow EEG waves (especially 1–10 Hz) increases.

Motion sickness in VR (visually induced motion sickness, VIMS) is attributed to a mismatch between visual and vestibular information, causing ambiguity about body position relative to the environment.
A clinical study exists that evaluates fluid-filled glasses for motion sickness symptom mitigation in a computer-assisted rehabilitation environment.

A study using galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS) in 10 participants demonstrated that "Beneficial" GVS produced a 26% motion sickness reduction and "Detrimental" GVS produced a 56% increase (p = 0.0055), confirming the causal role of vestibular sensory conflict in motion sickness.
Slow, intermittent exposure to motion can help reduce motion sickness symptoms.

A clinical study of 30 motion sickness-susceptible participants evaluated fluid-filled glasses (creating an artificial moving horizon) against a placebo group in a computer-assisted rehabilitation environment (CAREN), measuring symptoms with the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire before, after, and at 60-second intervals.
The clinical study measured motion sickness symptoms using the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire before, after, and at 60-second intervals during a simulated motion exposure.
Slow, intermittent exposure to motion and reducing physical, mental, or emotional discomfort are recommended preventive strategies for motion sickness.
Motion sickness is primarily caused by a sensory conflict or mismatch between vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive signals integrated in the brain.
Motion sickness is generally evoked from a mismatch in sensory cues between vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive signals integrated in the brainstem and cerebellum.
